awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Development of a Microfluidic Device for Multi-Omics Diagnosis of Cancer
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project lies in its potential to save lives by enabling earlier cancer diagnosis, which is known to significantly improve treatment outcomes and survival. Despite this, there are currently no effective early diagnostic tools for many types of cancer. Head and neck cancer is one such disease, with rising incidence and mortality rates, particularly among men. It is often detected late, typically during routine exams, only after symptoms become evident, by which point treatment options are limited and outcomes are poor. This project seeks to change that by developing a non-invasive, saliva-based test that can deliver accurate results within 30 minutes at the point of care. This approach could dramatically reduce the time to diagnosis, eliminate the need for invasive biopsies, and expand access to early cancer detection. By reducing the burden of late-stage diagnosis and enabling timely intervention, this innovation has the potential to lower healthcare costs, improve quality of life, and address significant gaps in health equity. Its modular design also allows for future adaptation to detect other cancers.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to develop and validate a portable diagnostic system that detects cancer markers for both risk and progression in saliva. The research will focus on creating a fully integrated microfluidic device that combines multiple types of biomarker detection into one enclosed cartridge. The project will address key technical challenges such as improving the consistency of sample handling, ensuring even distribution of reagents, and optimizing the materials and layout to support accurate, reliable results. The system will be tested using samples with known cancer markers to confirm performance against standard laboratory methods. The anticipated outcome is a working prototype that demonstrates the technical feasibility of delivering multi-biomarker analysis from a single non-invasive sample at the point of care.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Cancers of the head and neck are the sixth most common cancers worldwide, and most are found late. Early disease is hard to see during an ordinary examination, and a definitive answer requires a surgical biopsy, a painful procedure that needs a specialist, a pathology laboratory, and often several appointments spread over weeks. Survival drops sharply when these cancers are found late, and many patients, particularly in rural and under-resourced communities, never complete that path in time.

A large share of these cancers is linked to human papillomavirus (HPV). Testing for the virus alone does not answer the question, because most HPV infections are common and clear on their own without ever causing cancer. What distinguishes a dangerous infection is how the patient's own cells have changed in response to it. Detecting the virus and that cellular response together, from a single sample, is the idea behind this project.

Before this award, InnoTech had developed the laboratory chemistry to make those measurements from saliva in a test tube. The purpose of this NSF Small Business Innovation Research Phase I project was to move that chemistry out of the laboratory and into a small, sealed plastic cartridge that a clinician could use in an ordinary office.

The team built a detailed computer simulation of how liquid and air move through such a cartridge, and used it to work out the shapes of the chambers, where the air vents should sit, and what air pressure would move fluid reliably without forcing it where it should not go. Guided by that model, more than twenty cartridge versions were built and tested. Chambers filled in roughly three seconds each, matching what the simulation had predicted, and the finished cartridge needs only about 150 microliters of saliva, roughly three drops, and half of what the project had set as its target.

One of the most useful results came from a failure. An early cartridge was printed in clear resin, which turned out to glow under the same light used to read the test, drowning out the signal the cartridge was meant to detect. The team rebuilt the cartridge as a five-layer sandwich with a light-blocking black core and clear windows only where the reading is taken, which reduced that background glow to less than five percent of the signal. This is a practical finding for anyone building this kind of device, since clear plastic is the obvious first choice.

The finished cartridge was then tested against the established laboratory version of the same test. Across eight paired samples, the two systems agreed: every sample the laboratory method found positive was positive in the cartridge, and every negative was negative. The signal measured inside the cartridge is weaker than in the laboratory instrument, which is expected, because the cartridge was read under a microscope rather than through the purpose-built reader that will accompany it. Building that reader is one of the main goals of the next phase of work. No patient samples were used at any stage of this project; all saliva was purchased from commercial suppliers.

Alongside the laboratory work, the team interviewed more than a hundred ear, nose and throat specialists, oral surgeons, dentists and other stakeholders through the NSF I-Corps program. Those conversations sharpened what the test should do. Most patients sent for a biopsy of a suspicious area turn out not to have cancer, while the smaller number who do can wait several months for a confirmed diagnosis. Clinicians said they did not want a replacement for the biopsy; they wanted help deciding, during the visit, which patients need one urgently. That is the role the test is now being developed to fill.
